We have carbon NMR data: chemical shifts list: 138.76, 131.45, 131.45, 130.59, 130.59, 121.30, 43.47, 38.60.

We need number of CH3 groups (methyl). Typically methyl carbons appear around 10-30 ppm for aliphatic, but here we have 43.47 and 38.60 which could be CH3 attached to heteroatoms or aromatic? Also aromatic carbons around 120-140 ppm are sp2 carbons (likely aromatic ring). So the molecule likely has an aromatic ring (6 carbons) plus two aliphatic carbons at 43.47 and 38.60. Those could be CH2 or CH3. Need to determine which are methyl. Methyl carbon chemical shift ~ 10-30 ppm for simple alkyl, but for methyl attached to aromatic (toluene) ~ 21 ppm. For methyl attached to heteroatom (OCH3) ~ 55 ppm. 43.47 could be a carbon attached to N (e.g., N-CH3) or carbonyl? 38.60 could be CH2.

We need number of CH3 groups. Could be 1 (if one methyl). But we need more info. Maybe we can get proton NMR to see methyl signals. Let's request proton NMR for the SMILES? We don't have SMILES. Could infer from carbon NMR: 6 aromatic carbons (some duplicates due to symmetry). The list includes duplicates: 131.45 appears twice, 130.59 appears twice. So maybe a monosubstituted benzene? For monosubstituted benzene, you'd have 6 aromatic carbons distinct, but symmetry reduces? Actually monosubstituted benzene has 6 distinct aromatic carbons. Here we have 6 aromatic signals (138.76, 131.45 (x2),130.59 (x2),121.30) that's 5 distinct values but 6 peaks (some duplicates). Could be para-disubstituted? That gives 4 distinct aromatic carbons, each duplicated. Here we have 5 distinct values, not matching. Could be ortho-disubstituted? That gives 6 distinct. Hmm.

We have two aliphatic carbons: 43.47 and 38.60. Likely one is CH3, one is CH2. Need to determine which is methyl. Methyl attached to aromatic (toluene) ~ 21 ppm, not 43. So maybe it's N-methyl (e.g., N,N-dimethyl aniline) gives ~40 ppm for N-CH3. So could be two N-CH3 groups? N,N-dimethyl aniline would have two methyls attached to N, each same environment, giving one signal for both (maybe 40 ppm). But we have two distinct aliphatic signals, so maybe one is N-CH3 (around 40) and the other is CH2 (around 38). But CH2 also around 30-40 if attached to aromatic.

Thus likely only one methyl group. Let's verify by retrieving proton shifts for methyl region? Could request proton NMR.
